\chapter{Only and Still}
\label{ch:ta-only-and-still}
\hlchaptermodality{62}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say only, still, soon, at once and first of all in Tamil.}

Complete TA-C62-first-of-all and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[maṭṭum]{\ta{மட்டும்} (maṭṭum) — only}

\label{lesson:TA-C62-only}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kāyccal} mean, and what did \emph{vali} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மட்டும்}}
\textbf{\ta{மட்டும்}} (\emph{maṭṭum}) — \textquotedblleft{}only\textquotedblright{}.

This and nothing beside it. Where English puts \emph{only} in front of the thing it limits, Tamil hangs \ta{மட்டும்} on the end of it: \ta{தண்ணீர்} \ta{மட்டும்} — water, and nothing else.

Telugu does the same job with \te{మాత్రమే} (\emph{mātramē}). The doubled \ta{ட்ட} in the middle is the one held twice, as in \ta{ஆகட்டும்}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maṭṭum}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{maṭṭum}, then \emph{taṇṇīr}, and put them in the Tamil order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மட்டும்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}only\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[iṉṉum]{\ta{இன்னும்} (iṉṉum) — still, yet}

\label{lesson:TA-C62-still}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{maṭṭum} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{இன்னும்}}
\textbf{\ta{இன்னும்}} (\emph{iṉṉum}) — \textquotedblleft{}still, yet\textquotedblright{}.

For something that has not finished, and for a bit more of it: \ta{இன்னும்} \ta{சிறிது}, a little more still. Kannada \ka{ಇನ್ನೂ} (\emph{innū}) is the same word; Telugu says \te{ఇంకా} (\emph{iṅkā}).

The \ta{ன்} doubled in the middle is the soft one — the alveolar \ta{ன}, not the curled \ta{ண} you have in \ta{கிண்ணம்}. Tamil keeps three of these apart and this word wants the middle one twice.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{iṉṉum}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{iṉṉum}, then \emph{siṟitu}, and say the two together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{இன்னும்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}still, yet\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sīkkiram]{\ta{சீக்கிரம்} (sīkkiram) — soon}

\label{lesson:TA-C62-soon}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{iṉṉum} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{சீக்கிரம்}}
\textbf{\ta{சீக்கிரம்}} (\emph{sīkkiram}) — \textquotedblleft{}soon\textquotedblright{}.

Soon, and quickly — Tamil lets one word carry nearness in \ta{நேரம்} and speed of doing together, and which one is meant comes out of the sentence around it.

Set it against \ta{பிறகு} and the pair covers the whole span: \ta{சீக்கிரம்} is the near end, \ta{பிறகு} the loose one that promises nothing. Kannada says \ka{ಬೇಗ} (\emph{bēga}).

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sīkkiram}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sīkkiram}, then \emph{piṟaku}, and say which of the two commits you
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{சீக்கிரம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}soon\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[uṭaṉē]{\ta{உடனே} (uṭaṉē) — at once}

\label{lesson:TA-C62-at-once}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{sīkkiram} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{உடனே}}
\textbf{\ta{உடனே}} (\emph{uṭaṉē}) — \textquotedblleft{}at once\textquotedblright{}.

Tighter than \ta{சீக்கிரம்}: not soon but now, with nothing allowed in between. It is the word that answers an instruction you intend to obey.

Say it ending long, on the \ta{ே}. That final length is doing the work — it is what makes the word press rather than merely inform.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the fourth pushes harder than the third.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{uṭaṉē}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sīkkiram}, then \emph{uṭaṉē}, and say which one leaves you no room
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{உடனே} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}at once\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mutalil]{\ta{முதலில்} (mutalil) — first of all}

\label{lesson:TA-C62-first-of-all}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{uṭaṉē} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{முதலில்}}
\textbf{\ta{முதலில்}} (\emph{mutalil}) — \textquotedblleft{}first of all\textquotedblright{}.

Before anything else. It puts an order on things that had none: \ta{முதலில்} \ta{தண்ணீர்}, \ta{பிறகு} \ta{சாதம்} — water to begin with, and the rice after.

With this one you can lay out a sequence end to end: \ta{முதலில்}, then \ta{உடனே} or \ta{சீக்கிரம்} for what follows fast, then \ta{பிறகு} for what can wait.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: only, still, soon, at once, and first of all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mutalil}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{maṭṭum}, \emph{iṉṉum}, \emph{sīkkiram}, \emph{uṭaṉē}, \emph{mutalil}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{முதலில்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}first of all\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
